entries.text: New, Open, Save, and Save As for .rms files.
Starts a new, empty .rms script in a new tab.
Opens an existing .rms script from disk.
Saves the current tab. Prompts for a location the first time, same as Save As.
Saves the current tab to a new or different location.
Undo, redo, cut, copy, paste, select all, find, find and replace, toggle comment, and toggle command layout.
Undoes the last edit, in Breakdown or Code alike, they share one undo history.
Redoes the last undone edit.
Cuts the current selection in the Code tab. Switches you there first if you're in Breakdown.
Copies the current selection in the Code tab. Switches you there first if you're in Breakdown.
Pastes the clipboard into the Code tab at the cursor. Switches you there first if you're in Breakdown.
Selects the whole script in the Code tab. Switches you there first if you're in Breakdown.
Opens the Code tab's find widget. Switches you there first if you're in Breakdown.
Opens the Code tab's find and replace widget. Switches you there first if you're in Breakdown.
Wraps or unwraps the selected lines in a block comment (RMS has no line-comment syntax). Switches you to the Code tab first if you're in Breakdown.
Flips the command under the cursor between one line and one attribute per line, same as Code: Toggle Command Layout in Settings > Hotkeys. Switches you to the Code tab first if you're in Breakdown.
App settings, grouped into tabs: General, Hotkeys, Theme, Breakdown, Code, Advanced Tools and Credits.
Links out to reference material for writing random map scripts.
Opens Zetnus's guide to the DE random map scripting language in your browser. This app's own command and attribute docs are drawn from it.
Builds a small map called Golden Hill from scratch, step by step, right in the Breakdown editor. Starts over from step 1 even if you've finished it before.

Builds the islands of a 1v1 tournament map called Comeer, and teaches how land grows and what stops it. Sets the preview to 1v1 on a Tiny map and leaves it that way. Starts over from step 1 even if you've finished it before.
A tour of the preview, reference table, status bar, generation settings and Advanced Tools, for someone who already writes RMS. Starts over from step 1 even if you've finished it before.
What changed in the newest release with something worth announcing.
The name of the currently open map, taken from its filename. Shows "Untitled Map" until you open or save a file.
When this map was last saved during this session. Shows a dash until you save at least once.
Shows your script as editable command blocks instead of raw code. Good for building without memorizing syntax.
The full code editor, with RMS syntax highlighting and hover docs.
Built-in tools that operate on your script.

Total resources across the whole map, read from the actual preview generation currently showing, not a theoretical count of what the script asks for (a create_object with number_of_groups 9999 usually means "fill the map", not "place 9999 objects", and this bar reports what fits). Includes wood forest terrains spawn automatically. Reseed or edit the script to see a different generation's figures. Figures are abbreviated to fit the bar, so hover one to read the exact amount.

The spread across this generation's own players: the least any one player received and the most, for placements the script tied to a specific player (set_place_for_every_player, or place_on_specific_land_id on that player's own land). A gap here means an unbalanced map, not an estimate.
Everything this generation placed that isn't owned by a specific player, including forest terrains' automatic tree wood, which belongs to nobody.

Shown when the map preview is drawing less than the whole script: "Pinned line N" means Current view is cut at a pin you set, "Current line N" means it's following your cursor instead. Switch to Final, or pin further down, to see the whole map.

Errors and warnings found by the parser in the current file, re-checked live as you type on the Code tab. The triangle is red when there is at least one error, yellow when the worst is a warning, and blue when there is only information. Click a squiggle in the editor to see the full message.
Report a Bug.
Suggest a Feature / Tutorial / Idea.
Downloads the new version and restarts the app. If the map has unsaved changes you are asked to save first.
Hides this until the next time the app starts. Nothing is downloaded and the current version keeps running.
How many players this map is generated for. Scales resources placed with set_place_for_every_player in the totals above.
The map size this script targets. The right column is the player count the game picks for that size by default.

The lobby's Team Positions box. Ticked, the game seats teammates next to each other, and a script testing TEAM_POSITIONS takes that branch. It also changes the random draws the game makes while placing players, so the preview's lands, hills and cliffs only match a real game at the same seed when this box matches that game's lobby. Ticked by default.

The name written into the Author row of the comment this app stamps at the top of a script it creates. Left blank it reads Unknown. Changing it renames the author of scripts saved from now on, not of ones already stamped.
Controls when these help popups appear: always on hover, only while holding ALT, or off entirely.

Constant names in RMS run long, and readouts such as the preview's tile panel are narrow. With this on, a name over six characters is drawn as its first three letters followed by an ellipsis, and hovering it shows the whole name. Turn it off to always see names in full, at the cost of more wrapping.

The shortcut for Save, shown here and next to Save in the File menu. Click Change and press a new combination. It must include Ctrl or Alt, so it can never collide with ordinary typing. Escape cancels without changing anything.

The shortcut for Save As, shown here and next to Save As… in the File menu. Click Change and press a new combination. It must include Ctrl or Alt, so it can never collide with ordinary typing. Escape cancels without changing anything.

The shortcut for New File, shown here and next to New in the File menu. Click Change and press a new combination. It must include Ctrl or Alt, so it can never collide with ordinary typing. Escape cancels without changing anything.

The shortcut for Open File, shown here and next to Open… in the File menu. Click Change and press a new combination. It must include Ctrl or Alt, so it can never collide with ordinary typing. Escape cancels without changing anything.

The shortcut for switching the preview between Current and Final. Click Change and press a new combination. It must include Ctrl or Alt, so it can never collide with ordinary typing. Escape cancels without changing anything.

The shortcut for re-rolling the preview's seed. Click Change and press a new combination. It must include Ctrl or Alt, so it can never collide with ordinary typing. Escape cancels without changing anything.

The shortcut for deleting the selected Breakdown card. Click Change and press a new combination. It must include Ctrl or Alt, so it can never collide with ordinary typing. Escape cancels without changing anything.

The shortcut for opening the Add Command picker in the Breakdown tab. Click Change and press a new combination. It must include Ctrl or Alt, so it can never collide with ordinary typing. Escape cancels without changing anything.
The shortcut for moving the selected Breakdown card above the card before it. Alt+Up by default, the same keys Monaco uses to move a line in the Code tab. It must include Ctrl or Alt.
The shortcut for moving the selected Breakdown card below the card after it. Alt+Down by default. It must include Ctrl or Alt.
The shortcut for inserting a copy of the selected Breakdown card directly below it. It must include Ctrl or Alt.
The shortcut for commenting out the selected Breakdown cards, or uncommenting them when every one is a comment. Ctrl+/ by default, the same keys the Code tab uses. It must include Ctrl or Alt.

The shortcut for toggling a command between one line and one attribute per line in the Code tab. Click Change and press a new combination. It must include Ctrl or Alt, so it can never collide with ordinary typing. Escape cancels without changing anything.

Steps through the tabs of whatever has focus: Preview and Reference in the side panel, the section tabs in Breakdown, or in Code, scrolling the next section to the top. Adding Shift steps backwards. Click Change and press a new combination, which must include Ctrl or Alt.
Flips between Advanced Tools and whichever of Breakdown or Code you were last in. Click Change and press a new combination, which must include Ctrl or Alt.
Settings that apply across the whole app, including how these help popups behave.
Every keyboard shortcut in the app, for files, the preview, Breakdown's cards, the Code tab and tab cycling. Each one can be rebound here.
Pick Light, Dark, or a theme you've saved, and customize colours and the code font. Changes preview live before you save them.

Switch the active theme, or save your current colour edits as a new one. Light and Dark are built in and can't be edited in place. Customize below, then Save as new theme. A theme you saved can be updated, renamed or deleted from here too.

Scales the app's text and spacing up or down together, menus, tabs and panels included, and isn't tied to which theme is active. Applies when you release the slider, not while dragging it, since resizing everything mid-drag moves the slider itself out from under the pointer. Monaco sets its own font size for the Code tab's editor text directly, so this doesn't reach it.

Every colour, the code editor's monospace font, and the scrollbar colours, grouped by what they control. Editing one applies it everywhere immediately, so you can see the effect before deciding to keep it.
Settings for the Breakdown editor: density and attribute order today, with more planned.
When on, Add Command, Add Comment and Add Template scroll the list to the new card. When off, the card is still added and opened, the list just stays where it is.

Hides attribute rows that are not in the code, so a busy command shows only what it uses. Nothing real is ever hidden. Which rows show is decided when a card opens, so unticking a box does not make its row vanish, and each card gets an Add Attribute search bar for the hidden ones.
Attributes that stay visible on every card even when unused. Type a name and press Enter or Add. Click the cross on a name to remove it.
What happens when you click an attribute shown on a collapsed card. Open the card and go to that attribute, or edit it right there on the summary line.

Sets the order a command card's attribute rows render in. Required first groups the attributes marked required in the reference data ahead of everything else, then sorts the rest by type (text, then number, then boolean). Alphabetical ignores type. File order matches the order attributes appear in the code, with ones not yet written appended at the end. Custom lets you drag rows into your own order per card.

Comfortable is the default spacing. Compact tightens the padding around cards and rows, and lets a wide-enough command card split its attributes into two columns, booleans on the right, everything else on the left.
Settings for the code editor's indentation and its resolve flash.
How many spaces one tab press or one indent level counts as, and whether pressing Tab actually inserts spaces or a real tab character. Applies to the Code tab's editor immediately.

Which keys take the highlighted entry of the suggestion list while you type. The first choice also makes Shift+Tab step back up the list. The third matches VS Code's default. Grey prediction text is always accepted with Tab.
Briefly tints a name you just typed green when it matches a built-in constant or one of your own #consts above it.

Shows grey text after the caret copied from your own script. After a line's first word, the rest of the closest earlier line like it. After a block command, its last block, or a common one from other maps when you have none, with each value a stop. Tab accepts, Ctrl+Right takes one word, typing replaces it.
Settings for the Advanced Tools pane, which hasn't been built yet.
Who maintains this app, and who its reference material comes from.
Global constants and directives (#define/#const/#include) that appear before the first section. The natural home for defining a map-wide constant.
A section name the parser doesn't recognize (likely a typo in a <SECTION_HEADER>). Its contents still render below so you can see and fix it.

Ticked sections show together in one list. Untick to leave this one out. The last ticked section stays. Ctrl-click a section name to add or remove it, Shift-click to show every section from the current one to it.
Shows every section in one list, the full script. Click again to go back to the section in focus.
Click to put this section in focus, so Add Command, Add Comment and Add Template write here. Works on an empty section too.
Behaviours that apply to the whole script, such as how player lands are placed, changes to object and terrain behaviour, AI behaviour and more.
Commands that shape each player's land mass.
Commands that add hills and elevation.
Commands that place cliffs.
Commands that paint additional terrain types onto the map.
Commands that connect player areas (roads, water paths) and their terrain along the way.
Commands that place resources, forests, and other objects.
Opens a searchable list of commands to insert into the section in focus. Filtered to that section by default. Toggle "show all sections" to search everything.
Search commands from every section, not just this tab's. RMS doesn't enforce section placement, so this is a convenience filter, not a restriction.
Type to filter the command list by name or description. Escape closes the picker.

Click a command to insert it. The two rows at the top, if and start_random, insert an empty block to fill with commands. The chip on the other rows shows whether this command's reference data has been verified against the official docs. "Unverified" entries may have incomplete or unconfirmed argument details, but are still safe to use.
Inserts a blank comment you can type into right away. It goes after the selected card, or at the end of this tab if nothing is selected, same placement rule as Add command.
Opens a dialog offering ready-made blocks of commands for this tab. Shown on the Objects and Terrain tabs.
A town center, starting villagers, and a scout for every player.
Berries, gold, stone, sheep, deer, and boar around every player's start.
Shore and deep-water fish placed once for the whole map, plus optional oysters and whales.
The exact script text Insert will add, updated as you change the options above.
Closes this dialog without changing the script.
Inserts the previewed block into the script and selects its first command.
The unit placed as each player's scout. Horse is a separate object from the scout cavalry unit, not a skin.

Swaps the plain villager block for a 9-villager quick start: six on a sheep next to the town center, three on the nearest forest, plus two houses. Placed behind if QUICK_START, with the plain three villagers as the else branch, and a #define QUICK_START is added to the file's header unless it has one.
Places the sheep and all nine villagers with the exact tile-reservation technique Venn.rms and Bulls_Eyes.rms use, instead of the simpler distance-based version. Only applies while quick-start is on.
When set, every command in this block gets terrain_to_place_on with this value. Leave blank to use each command's own default.
Emits the placeholder names the DE seasons include expects (HERDABLE, HUNTABLE, LURABLE, BERRIES) instead of fixed object names, and adds the include line for it.
Which bush the berry block places. None leaves the block out. Seasonal variation picks the name itself, so only Seasonal or None remain.
Which animal fills this role. None leaves its blocks out. Seasonal variation picks the name itself, so only Seasonal or None remain.
Includes the large gold pile. DE's standard is 7 objects, 12 to 16 tiles from the player.
Includes the small gold pile. DE's standard is 4 objects, placed further out.
Includes the large stone pile. DE's standard is 5 objects, 14 to 18 tiles from the player.
Includes the small stone pile. DE's standard is 4 objects, placed further out.
How many mines the pile holds (number_of_objects). A whole number above 0.
When set, every command in this block gets terrain_to_place_on with this value. Leave blank to use each command's own default.
Adds a water-placed oyster block.
Adds whales, a 2x2 gold pickup that lives in deep water.
A forest near every player, built from tree objects that each turn their own tile into forest terrain. Needs a few lines in PLAYER_SETUP, which are added for you.
A forest near every player, painted as real forest terrain one player at a time. Reads the player land terrain from create_player_lands.
A spare object reshaped into a one-tile forest maker. 1639 is the one the example maps use. Pick an id nothing else in your script places.
The terrain each placed stand-in leaves under its tile.
Any forest terrain name or id. A name your script defines with #const works as long as it is defined before the end of PLAYER_SETUP, where the setup lines go.
The tree shown on each tile, placed with second_object. None leaves second_object out, so only the forest terrain is painted.
Any object name or id to show on each forest tile, including one your script defines with #const.
How many separate forests each player gets.
How many trees, and so how many forest tiles, each forest has.
The closest a forest tile can be to the player's start.
The furthest a forest tile can be from the player's start.
Optional. Limits the forests to this terrain. Leave it empty and the stand-in can land anywhere it fits, water included for some stand-ins.
The terrain create_player_lands paints. Filled in from your script, change it if your player lands use a different terrain by the time terrain generation runs.
The forest terrain each player's forest is painted with.
Any forest terrain name or id, including one your script defines with #const before this point.
How many forest tiles each player gets in total.
How many separate forests those tiles are split into.
No forest tile is placed closer than this to the player's start.
No forest tile is placed further than this from the player's start.

Click +/− to expand this command and see or edit its arguments and attributes. The attributes listed here are clickable too. Ctrl+click adds the card to the selection, Shift+click selects a run of cards.
This command's inline comment, written on the same line as the command. Enter or click away to save, Escape to undo the typing.
An inline comment that spans lines or holds another comment. Edit it in the Code tab.
Removes this inline comment. Undo with Ctrl+Z.
Adds an inline comment on this command's line, e.g. create_land /* top left island */.

Click to open the card at this attribute, or to edit it right here, depending on the Breakdown setting for clicking a collapsed card's attributes. In edit mode, clicking a boolean attribute removes it and leaves it struck through for half a minute so one more click puts it back.
This boolean attribute was just removed from the code. Click to put it back. It disappears from the summary on its own after half a minute.
Hide Unused is on, so attributes this command does not use are out of sight. Type here to find one and click it to add it to the card.

Click anywhere on this left edge to collapse the card. The list scrolls so the collapsed card sits at the top, and reopening it without scrolling in between takes you back to where you were inside it.
Expands or collapses this command's arguments and attributes.
Removes this command (and its block) from the script. Undo with Ctrl+Z.
Wraps this card in /* */ so the game skips it. The card stays in the list as a comment and its own button puts it back. Ctrl+/ does the same for every selected card.
Takes the /* */ off, so the text runs as code again. Text that is not RMS shows up as raw cards. Ctrl+/ does the same when every selected card is a comment.
A positional argument this command takes. Commits when you click away or press Enter; Escape reverts.
This argument's name. Hover shows what it means, its range and its default, where the reference data has them.
Drag to reorder this attribute within the card. Only available with the Custom attribute order setting selected.
Saves the order you just dragged as the default for every command of this name, so it's remembered the next time this map (or any map) opens.
This attribute's current value, taken directly from the code. Commits when you click away or press Enter; Escape reverts to the current value.
Empties this field so you can type or pick a fresh value. Nothing changes in the code until you click away or press Enter.
This attribute's name. Hover shows what it does, sourced from the reference docs.
A checkbox attribute. Checked means the flag is present in the code, unchecked means it's absent. Toggling adds or removes the flag immediately.
This attribute appears more than once in the code, so every instance is listed and edited independently. None of them are merged or overwritten.
Not present in the code yet. This faint row is a placeholder, not real content. Clicking + inserts the attribute into the code.
Removes this attribute (or this one instance of it, if it appears more than once) from the code. Undo with Ctrl+Z.
Adds another instance of this repeatable attribute.
A recognized attribute that isn't in this command's usual list, but is still valid and editable.
An if/elseif/else block. Each branch's contents render below it and are fully editable. Drag any card onto an empty branch, or between the cards in one, to put it under the condition.
The label this branch runs under (a game mode, a #define you made, etc). Commits on blur/Enter; free text is always accepted.
Adds a command inside this branch.
Inserts a copy of this card directly below it, text for text, comments included. The copy is selected afterwards, so duplicating again stacks copies downward.
Swaps this card with the one above it. Greyed out at the top of its section or branch. To move a card further, or into an if branch, drag it by its header.
Swaps this card with the one below it. Greyed out at the bottom of its section or branch.
Deletes this card and everything inside it, the same as its trash button. With several cards selected, deletes them all. Undo with Ctrl+Z.
Wraps this card in /* */ so the game skips it, the same as its /* button. With several cards selected, comments out each of them.
Add another elseif or an else branch (only one else is allowed).
Removes this whole if/elseif/else block, including all its branches.
Removes just this branch. Disabled when it's the only branch left. Delete the whole conditional instead.
A start_random block. Each percent_chance branch has a weight and its own contents; exactly one branch runs when the map generates.

This branch's percent_chance weight. Commits on blur/Enter. Starts blank rather than 0, since a first branch declared percent_chance 0 is an engine bug (it still runs) rather than a way to disable the branch.
Adds a command inside this branch.
Adds another percent_chance branch.
Removes this whole start_random/end_random block, including all its branches.
Removes just this branch. Disabled when it's the only branch left. Delete the whole random block instead.
A preprocessor directive like #define or #const. Commits on blur/Enter; a quoted filename argument (#include_drs/#includeXS) keeps its quotes automatically.
This directive is accepted by the game but does nothing in Definitive Edition. Safe to leave, but it won't have any effect.
Removes this code from the script. For a shared block that includes the cards inside it.
Removes this attribute line from the script.
Removes this directive line from the script.
Warnings you have hidden, and the buttons that bring them back.
Warnings you turned off everywhere with "Don't show me this again". Each stays hidden in every file until you turn it back on here.
Shows this warning again, in every file where it applies.
Warnings you hid with Ok, which hides a warning in that one file only. Show them again brings back every one of them, in every file.
Hides this warning in this file. It still appears in other files. Settings, Diagnostics brings it back.
Turns this warning off in every file. Settings, Diagnostics turns it back on.
A problem somewhere in this card, coloured by its worst severity. Click to jump straight to it.
A comment from your script. Click into it to edit the text. It can't contain /* or */, since those would end or unbalance the comment.
Expands or collapses this comment. Collapsed shows just its first line.
Removes this comment from the script. Undo with Ctrl+Z.
A comment containing another comment inside it. Shown for reference only. Switch to the Code tab to change it.
This comment holds code, shown as cards you can still edit. Text shows the comment as plain text, Cards switches back.
Adds a #const row below with its name selected for typing over. Enter from the last value lands here, Enter again adds the row.
Adds a #define row below with its name selected for typing over. Enter from the last name lands here, Enter again adds the row.

This code couldn't be shown as an editable block, usually because it's unusual/exotic RMS the parser intentionally leaves alone rather than risk misrepresenting it. The exact text from your file is shown below, unchanged.
Expands or collapses this raw code region. Collapsed shows just its first line.
Applies the suggested spelling in place. The region usually turns into a normal editable card once it re-parses.
This command name isn't recognized, but it's close to a known one. Applies the suggested spelling in place. The card usually turns into a fully recognized command once it re-parses.
Jumps to this exact spot on the Code tab so you can edit it directly.
An attribute written outside any command's { } block. It has no effect where it sits. Move it inside the intended command's block.
Opens Generation Settings over the map: map size, player count and teams, used to compute the resource totals and this preview. Ctrl+D does the same by default while focus is in the map preview.
Closes Generation Settings. Esc does the same while focus is in the map preview.

Switches the map preview between Truncate at Cursor (on) and the whole script (off). Truncate at Cursor draws only what the script has built up to your cursor, so you can see what a half written script produces. The code it leaves out is dimmed, and the pin button beside this holds the cut point still while you edit elsewhere. The preview draws your actual script, generated in the background as you edit.
Switches the reference table below between Terrain constants, Object constants and Commands / Attributes.

Filters the table below to rows containing what you type, matching anywhere in any column the table shows. The text carries across the three lists, so you can type a name once and check whether it is a terrain or an object. Escape clears it.

Changes the table's order. Terrain and Objects sort by descriptive name, RMS constant or constant id. Commands sort by section, in the order sections run in a script, or by name, which also sorts each command's attributes. The arrow flips the direction.

The Objects tab lists every unit in the game's gaia roster, and about 500 of those are carcasses and blood decals: what a unit turns into when it dies, rather than something a script places. They are hidden until you tick this. Nothing is removed: a script can still reach one by its ID number, and the search box finds it once the rows are showing.

A read-only lookup of the constants/commands available in RMS, sourced from this app's reference data. In Commands / Attributes, click a command's arrow to see the attributes it accepts inside its block; searching for an attribute opens its command automatically. Some columns are placeholders pending later data-extraction work.
Cancels the action. Age of RMS stays as it is and nothing is saved or discarded.
Cancels the action, exactly like the Cancel button. Pressing Esc or clicking outside the dialog does the same.
Saves this map first, then continues with what you were doing (closing, opening another map or updating). If the map has never been saved, you'll be asked where to put it.
Continues WITHOUT saving. Every change made since the last save is permanently discarded.

Common lobby setups. Selecting one takes over the team assignments (and the player count, except for FFA). Press the same button again to release it and get your own configuration back, or just type a different player count to release it that way.
This player's team. Left click to advance through - 1 2 3 4, right click to go back. "-" means no team. Teams are capped at 4 because the game's script conditionals are.

How the game will actually read this lobby. Team numbers are renumbered by lobby order rather than the number you picked, and a team with only one player is not counted as a team at all, so a 1v1 reports no teams.

The approximate map preview. Drag to pan, use the wheel to zoom around the pointer, double click to fit the whole map. Hovering a tile shows its terrain, elevation and anything placed on it underneath. Clicking a tile pins that readout so it stays put while you move the pointer away; clicking the same tile again unpins it.
Unpins the selected tile, so the readout follows the pointer again. Clicking the selected tile on the map does the same thing.

Sets the point Current stops at. Put your cursor where you want the map to stop, then click this to hold the preview there while you keep editing and moving around; click it again to let go, and Current follows your cursor instead. Everything after that point is dimmed in the code and left out of the map, down to the individual attribute, so you can watch a land take shape as you add lines to it. A pin sticks to the code it was set in, so edits above it move it along with them.

The map size this preview was drawn at, in tiles, and the player count it was generated for. Both come from the generation settings (the gear button), except that a script using override_map_size changes the size here mid-script, so this can differ from the size you picked.

The random seed this arrangement was drawn from. The same seed always produces the same preview, so a number can be shared and reproduced. It is also the game's own seed for the lands, hills and cliffs. Type the seed a match used (the game shows it on the Objectives screen) with the same players, teams and Team Positions setting, and those come out where the game put them. Everything drawn after the cliffs is the preview's own approximation and will differ.
Draws a new seed and generates a fresh arrangement. Rolling through several is how you tell a layout that holds up from one that got lucky once.
Saves exactly what the map preview is currently showing as a PNG image: this zoom, this pan, this Current/Final view. Opens a save dialog first, so nothing is written until you pick a location.
Shows how to use the map: click a tile to pin it, drag to pan, wheel to zoom, double click to fit. Click again to close.
Everything the preview did not simulate, plus every placement that failed. Worth opening before trusting a layout, because a quiet map is not the same as a correct one.

How many placements the preview could not make. A failure usually means the script asked for something the map cannot supply, such as a resource on a terrain that was never generated. The Notes box lists one line per command per kind of failure, with a count beside it, rather than one line per attempt. A single command can fail tens of thousands of times and they all have the same cause.

The four coloured tiles. Which set of terrain colours to draw with, and the tiles show the set in use. Off is Game, which uses the average colour of each terrain's own texture from your install, so snow looks like snow; terrains that share a texture file, such as Forest and Underbrush, share a colour. On is Minimap, which uses the colour class stored in the game's own data, which is flatter and only has twelve colours in it, so every snow terrain comes out grass green, but it does tell forest apart from underbrush.

Which terrain each colour stands for, and where the colour came from. A row is marked when its colour did not come from the mode you selected, which happens when the reference data has no colour for that terrain.
Zooms in on the middle of the view. The mouse wheel zooms around the pointer instead, which is usually what you want.
Zooms out from the middle of the view.
Fits the whole map back into the panel. Double clicking the map does the same thing.

Drag this edge to make the map panel wider or narrower, or click the arrow to hide it and give the whole tab to the code. Dragging it well past its narrowest hides it too. Arrow keys resize it once it has focus. The width is shared by the Breakdown and Code tabs and is remembered between sessions.
Brings the map panel back at the width you last left it.
Shows the map preview.
Shows the reference table of terrains, objects, commands and attributes.

Lists every object your script names, how many this generation placed, and a tick box to hide each one from the map. A count of zero means nothing could be placed, usually because no tile met its terrain or distance rules. A warning triangle shows here while anything is hidden.
Filters the list to objects whose name or count contains what you type. Escape clears it.
Orders the list by object name or by how many were placed. The arrow flips the direction. Sorting by count can move rows when you re-roll.
Re-ticks every object at once, so the map draws everything again. Shown only while something is hidden.

Untick to hide this object from the map above, which is the quickest way to see what is underneath a few thousand trees. It only changes the drawing: the objects are still placed, still counted in this table, and still listed when you click their tile. A warning triangle appears on the Obj. List button while anything is hidden.
Picks which tool runs. Switching tools while one is running cancels it first. Only one tool runs at a time.
Runs the selected tool against the open script. If you just typed, the script is re-parsed first so the tool never reads stale code.
Asks the tool to stop. A well-behaved tool stops within a moment; one that ignores the request is shut down after 60 seconds and reported as not having behaved.
Run settings for the selected tool. These come from the tool itself, so each tool shows a different form.
How far along the run is. A bar that slides without filling means the tool has not said how much work is left.
What the tool reported. Rows and links that point at code jump the Code tab to that spot.
Applies the changes the tool proposed, as a single undo step. Disabled if the code changed since the tool ran. Re-run instead.
Problems the host found with what the tool sent, and anything the tool wrote to its error stream.

Things about this script that limit what Land Placement can manage: code the app can only show as raw text, a random parameter emitted for a different player count, or a fence that could not be read. Empty on a healthy script.
The seed the panel's own preview is drawn from, separate from Breakdown and Code's seed, so switching tabs never resets it. Re-roll to see a different arrangement at the pinned seed.
Adds a new role: a shared set of terrain, size, elevation and land-percent values that any number of lands can wear. Editing a role's fields edits every land wearing it.

Adds a shape (a circle to start, changeable to line, arc, square, triangle or polygon) of lands around the map centre, evenly spaced, all wearing the role picked in the with role list. With (none) picked it places points instead, which other lands can be parented to or chained off. Set the radius, rotation, repeat count and origin once it's created.
Adds one standalone land, not part of any shape, for a single feature like a home base or a lone resource pocket.

Radial measures this land's angle at its parent, from the ray pointing back at the parent's own anchor, so the whole chain turns together when a root turns. Absolute uses a plain world bearing instead. Radial only has an angle to measure from when the parent itself is polar (a circle, line or arc member, or another radial/absolute polar land). Parented to a square, triangle or polygon member (or anything cartesian/formula), it falls back to a plain bearing and behaves exactly like absolute.

Land positions, drawn live from the numbers on the right. The map underneath is a real generation at the panel's own pinned seed, cut at the end of land placement. Click a land to select it; drag to pan, wheel to zoom.

Every land and chain anchor in this layout, indented to show which placement each one is measured from. The columns give its label, the shape it belongs to (blank for a standalone land), its role, and any overrides or a detached warning. Click a row to select it. Its editor opens under this list and the map highlights it.
Deletes this land. Only offered for a standalone land; a land that belongs to a shape is deleted with the whole shape, from the Shapes section.

Every shape in this layout, with how many lands it places and the roles those lands wear. A shape is named by its kind and a number, and the number matches the one in its lands' labels (Square 2 places ring_2_0_slot_3 and so on). Click a shape to edit its radius, rotation, repeats and pattern under this list. The map highlights its lands and shows its rotation and radius handles.
Deletes this shape and every land it places.
Selects the shape this land belongs to and opens its editor in the Shapes section.

The selected land's own numbers. A standalone land sets its parent, frame (radial or absolute), offset and role here. A land that belongs to a shape takes its parent, frame and radius from the shape, so only its angle and role are set here. Edit shape opens the shape itself.

The shape this ring's lands are arranged in. Circle spaces them evenly around the radius. Line runs them through the anchor, signed by radius, with Radius shown as the line's own half length. Arc is a circle stopped short, with a Sweep field for how many degrees it spans. Square, Triangle and Polygon all walk their own perimeter, landing on a corner or an edge depending on the count. Rotation works the same way for every shape, including a formula that re-rolls each generation. Polygon adds a Sides field for how many corners it has. Every shape works with One land per player. Switching a shape with jitter in degrees to Line, Square, Triangle or Polygon turns the jitter into a percent of the even gap at the player count being previewed, since those shapes have no angle along them.

How many sides this polygon has, from 3 up to 12. Past a dozen sides a polygon and a circle look the same at map scale, and Circle gets there with less arithmetic, so this stops short of offering more.

Slides this land along the shape's perimeter, as a percent of one full lap around it, added on top of its even spacing. A polygon's corners sit further from the centre than its edges, so sliding a land along the shape also changes how far out it sits, not only which way it faces. Signed, and past 100 just wraps around for another lap.

How close to each map edge a land wearing this role may grow, as a percent of the map. Placement of a positioned land ignores borders, but growth does not, so a land placed outside its borders stays at its base size. Leave a side empty to write nothing and let the engine use its default. Negative values are legal as long as the land's origin is still inside the map. The guide notes that a top border larger than the others can misbehave on player lands, so pair it with another side.
How ragged the edge of each land wearing this role is, 0 to 100. Empty writes nothing, and the placeholder shows the engine's own default.
How blobby each land wearing this role grows. Higher is rounder and stays in one piece; lower is stringier and can fragment. Empty writes nothing, and the placeholder shows the engine's own default.
The gap, in tiles, each land wearing this role keeps from lands in other zones. Empty writes nothing.
A number objects can target later with place_on_specific_land_id. Written last in each land, after the player assignment, because assigning a land resets its id. Empty writes nothing.

Makes each land wearing this role start from a round base instead of a square one. When combined with an elevation the guide reports the whole square is raised; setting Conformity to 99 is the documented fix.

How closely each land wearing this role follows its base shape. The guide calls this attribute buggy and advises against it in general, except as the fix for a circular base raised by base_elevation, where 99 is the value to use. Empty writes nothing.

Writes direct_placement under the script's <PLAYER_SETUP> header, opening that section if there is none. Without it the engine arranges player lands in its own circle and ignores every position this tool writes.
Adds an empty <ELEVATION_GENERATION> section after the land section. The section only has to exist for base_elevation to take effect; it can stay empty.

Gives this one land its own value for an attribute its role sets, without duplicating the role. The land keeps following the role on everything else. The script gets one extra constant named after this land, and the land's create_land references that instead of the role's.

Removes this override so the land follows its role again. This deletes the override rather than copying the role's current value into it, which would leave the land looking as if it still followed the role while actually frozen.

Adds a land that hangs off every land this slot places, one copy per repeat, so a ring of eight player lands gets eight of these, each measured from its own player land. Edit it here once and every copy follows. This is how a cluster of lands around each player is built.
The label and role of this chained land. The label is the stem of the emitted constant names; the role is shared by every copy.
Radial measures the angle from the ray pointing back at the member's own anchor, so the cluster turns with the ring. Absolute uses a plain world bearing.

How far from its member and at what angle this chained land sits, in the member's own frame. A formula or a random parameter is allowed. Dragging one copy on the map nudges only that copy; editing here restates every un-nudged copy.

Removes this chained land from the pattern. Copies that have been dragged, have a child of their own, or are referenced elsewhere in the script are kept as ordinary lands rather than deleted, and the strip says which.

The random draws this layout hoists into the script, each emitted once as a #const with rnd(min,max). Every new shape gets a ROTATION parameter so the map differs from seed to seed. Reference one from any formula field by its name, or type rnd(a,b) into a field to create a new one.
One draw per player instead of one shared draw, so each player's lands get their own value. Only a land that belongs to a player, or hangs off one, can use a per-player parameter.
Removes this random parameter. Refused while any field still references it, since the script would then name a constant that does not exist.
Adds a shared random parameter with a placeholder range. Rename it, set its range, then reference it by name from a formula field.

The role the next shape, land or pattern slot is created with. Change it here before pressing + Shape, + Land or + slot, or change a land's or slot's role afterwards in its own editor. Falls back to the first role if the chosen one is deleted. With (none), + Land makes a chain anchor, a land with no role that writes no create_land but can be a parent for other lands. + Shape is off with (none), since a shape needs a role for its lands, and + slot uses the first role.

The role every land placed from this slot wears. Pick (none, points) to place points instead of lands. A point is written to the script as a position only, with no create_land, and other lands can be parented to it or chained off it. Changing the role re-dresses those lands in place, and lands you have dragged keep their nudge. A pattern can mix roles, so a ring can alternate player lands with neutral ones.

Adds another land to one repeat of this shape's pattern, wearing the role picked in the with role list, or a point when (none) is picked. A pattern is the cycle of lands the shape goes round with, so two slots on a ring of 4 repeats places 8 lands, alternating between the two. Lands you have already dragged keep their nudge when the pattern changes.

Takes this land out of the pattern. Any land that was placed from it and has no chained child, no drag of its own and nothing else in the script referring to its constants is removed with it; anything that fails one of those is released as an ordinary land instead of deleted, and the strip below says which.

Makes this shape produce one land per player instead of a fixed count. At generation time the script reads how many players are in the game and spreads that many lands over the whole shape, correct at every count. On an Arc or a Line the lands always reach both ends, so 3 players sit at the two ends and the middle. On a Square, Triangle or Polygon they spread evenly round the perimeter. While this is on, Repeats follows the game's own player count instead of a number you set. It works with every shape.

This land's angle at specific player counts, on top of the rule above. Each row overrides the angle only at the player count it names; every other count still uses the rule above. Free bearings (a random angle with no reference to another player) can still collide, since nothing in the script can guarantee separation between two independent random draws. On a Square, Triangle or Polygon a bearing alone does not pick a point on the perimeter, so the list shows there only for a land that already has an override, say from a shape change, and only lets it be removed. While the land keeps one it takes no jitter at any count.

The closest two neighbouring lands on this ring may come once jitter is added, in degrees around the ring. The jitter offered below is sized so this holds at every player count, which means it is worked out at 8 players, where the even spacing is tightest. Refuses rather than guessing when 8 players leave no room for it.

Degrees moves a land by up to the same number of degrees at every player count. Percent of the even gap scales with the count, so at 2 players a land can move further than at 8, and one percentage is equally safe at both. On an Arc the even gap is the sweep divided by one less than the number of lands. A Line, Square, Triangle or Polygon has no angle along it, so its jitter is always a percent of the gap and this choice is hidden.

How far each player's land may move, as a whole number of at least 1. On a Line it is always a percent of the even gap, the line's full length divided by one less than the number of lands. On a Square, Triangle or Polygon it is always a percent of the even gap round the perimeter, and a land turns the corner when the amount carries it past one. In degrees it is the most a land moves along the arc. In percent it is a share of the even gap between neighbours at each player count, so two neighbours close by at most twice the amount as a share of their gap, and an amount under 50 never lets them meet at any count. In degrees the gap is smallest at 8 players, where it is the sweep divided by one less than 8 times the number of slots. Nothing caps the amount. Past 50 percent lands can pass each other, and the two end lands can move past the ends of the arc or the line.

Moves each player's land by its own random amount, up to the size shown, every time the map generates. On a Circle the size is the largest safe amount worked out above. On any other shape it is the amount you typed. Each player gets one draw, so a player's lands in a pattern with several slots move together. On a Circle or an Arc, a land with its own angle, or a per count override, stays exactly where you put it. On a Line the jitter slides a land along the line, so only a land with its own distance, or one you dragged, stays put. On a Square, Triangle or Polygon the jitter walks a land along the perimeter and round its corners, and a land you dragged, one with its own angle or distance, or one with a per count angle stays put. Press it again to change the amount.
Takes the jitter off this ring and deletes its random parameter, so every player sits on the even spacing again.

The point this shape is centred on, the map centre by default. Pick any land to centre the shape on it, including a points only land or a land in another shape, and the shape follows it wherever it moves. A shape cannot be centred on one of its own lands, or on anything hanging off them.

Makes a new point with no land on it, at this shape's current centre, and centres the shape on it. The shape does not move until the point does. Drag the point on the map, or edit its distance and angle, to move the shape.

Absolute keeps the shape facing the same way wherever its origin goes, so Rotation is a plain map bearing. Radial measures the shape's angles from the direction back toward its origin's own parent, so the shape turns as its origin moves around that parent. That suits a small ring that should always face away from the map centre. Moving the origin never changes this for you. New shapes start radial.

Every role this layout uses, with its terrain and how many lands wear it. Click a role to edit it under this list, and the map highlights the lands wearing it. A role's terrain, size, elevation, extent, zone and player assignment are shared by every land wearing it. Change one line and every one of those lands follows.
Deletes this role. Lands wearing it keep their position but lose the terrain, size, elevation, extent, zone and player assignment it gave them.

How big each land wearing this role grows, as either a percent of the map (land_percent) or a tile count (number_of_tiles). The script can only carry one of the two on a land, so this is one choice with one value, and switching keeps the number you typed.

Which zone each land wearing this role belongs to. A fixed zone puts every one of them in the same zone. Per repeat gives each land in a ring its own zone, counted up from the base by the step. set_zone_randomly lets the engine pick. Lands in the same zone are allowed to touch; lands in different zones keep apart.

Whether lands wearing this role belong to a player. assign_to_player takes a player number. assign_to takes a target kind (a player number, a colour, or a team), the number, and the engine's mode and flags, usually 0 and 0. The number can count up per repeat, so a ring hands one land to each player, or be fixed, including a constant the script already defines. Any assignment here needs direct_placement in the script, or the engine ignores the position.

Everything Apply would write: the fenced #const block that goes in the script's header, and the create_land command for every land, guards included. Nothing here touches the document until Apply is pressed.

Writes the current layout into the script as a single undo step. The fenced #const block goes in the script's header; each create_land goes in <LAND_GENERATION>, which is created in its proper place if the script has none. Once a fence exists the button reads Update: a land the tool wrote and you have not touched is rewritten in place when its role changes, a land you have edited by hand is left alone, and re-applying with no changes makes zero edits.
Opens a walkthrough of the whole tool. What it writes into the script, why an existing hand-written layout starts empty here, the order to build a layout in, and what every canvas gesture does.
Closes the walkthrough. Escape and a click outside the box do the same thing.
Goes back one step. Never disabled once you're past the first.
Moves to the next step. Works even if this step isn't done yet. Nothing here is enforced.
Moves on without doing this step. Mechanically the same as Next.
Ends the tutorial without marking it finished. Nothing you've written is touched.
Shrinks this card to a small bar in the bottom right corner and turns off the spotlight, so you can work without it in the way. The next step opens it again.
Opens the whole step again.
Drag here to move this card. It keeps that spot for the rest of the tutorial, except on a step where it would cover what the step is pointing at.
A step for trying things and watching the preview. Some changes here are put back later.
A step that adds something to your finished script.
Adds these commands for you, exactly as described, so you can see the result and move on.
Picks how the rest of this tutorial runs. Go Back to this step to change it.
Starts a short tour of what's new, spotlighting the new controls.
Dismisses this announcement. You can still find it from Help ▸ What's new.
Opens the maintainer's Buy Me a Coffee page in your browser. Entirely optional.
Opens the maintainer's Buy Me a Coffee page in your browser. Entirely optional.
Opens the RMS Discord invite in your browser, not inside the app.
Starts the "New to RMS" tutorial. Builds a small map from scratch, step by step.
Starts the "New to the tool" tutorial: a quick tour of the preview, reference and tools.
Closes this pane without starting either tutorial. Find them again any time from Help.
Names that fit this field, best match first. Tab or Down moves the highlight, Shift+Tab or Up moves it back, Enter accepts it, Escape closes the list. Enter before moving keeps what you typed.
Replaces what you typed with the built-in name it is closest to.
The number to give the new #const. It starts at the value of the nearest built-in name.
Where the new #const line goes. Above this command keeps it next to its use, the header makes it available to the whole script.
Writes the #const line. Ctrl+Z removes it.
Hides this offer. Nothing in the script changes.
Moves the #const line to just above this command, so the game sees it here. Ctrl+Z puts it back.
Briefly tints a field green when the name you typed matches a built-in constant or one of your own #consts above it. The same switch as in Settings > Code.
Copies the lines above to the clipboard. Paste them into the Code or Breakdown tab, outside the fenced block, and give each name its real value.
